items.title: Spiegle Willcox and Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Norwich, New York, November 14, 1995
items.q: he had a lot to do with me emulating him and so forth... So Rudy Wiedoeft meant a lot to me, yes. I emulated him

ctx.x: Yeah? That’s great. When you were young boys and you were hearing music around your house, what was it that was being played? Can you describe the music that you heard?

All right. I can remember, I’m born in 1913 and we’ll say 1923, I first heard the famous Rudy Wiedoeft on records. ‘78s. And my father took me to Forbes Music Store in Birmingham, Alabama. I never forgot Forbes, it’s still there. Different owners of course. And naturally I marveled at Rudy Wiedoeft. And he had a lot to do with me emulating him and so forth. And I studied hard. And my father got me my first saxophone when I was twelve. And it was called “Perfect Tone” would you believe it? I don’t know who it was…
It’s obvious that the classical part of music has been a big influence on you too. I can hear it in your playing.

items.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005
items.q: My father bought me Rudy Wiedoeft records... I’ll never forget the first time I heard Rudy Wiedoeft play

ctx.x: Exactly. My father bought me Rudy Wiedoeft records. Yes, Forbes Music in Birmingham, I’ll never forget the first time I heard Rudy Wiedoeft play “Saxophobia” or “Valse Vanite,” which I have on the thing — you have it. I did that live at NBC with the orchestra back around 1943, 44. And if I have to say so myself that’s very good. Live performance. All my life, JoAnn can tell you, you rarely hear fluff. I was a perfectionist. Actually I was a perfectionist.
How did you get home every day from these engagements in the evening in New Orleans. Did someone have to take you back and forth or did you take a cable car?
